+------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| Objectives                                                             |
+========================================================================+
| -   Learn what continuous integration (CI) is and why it's useful.     |
| -   Write GitHub Actions workflows to automatically run unit tests.    |
| -   Use GitHub Actions to build and deploy a website to GitHub Pages.  |
+------------------------------------------------------------------------+

[GitHub Actions](https://docs.github.com/en/actions) is GitHub's tool for
automating tasks in your repository. You tell GitHub what to do (e.g., "install
my package and run the tests") and when to do it (e.g., "every time someone
opens a pull request") by writing a *workflow* file. GitHub then runs the
workflow for you on one of its computers (called a *runner*) and reports the
results back to you.

This is incredibly useful for open source projects. Two common uses are:

-   **Continuous integration (CI)**: automatically running your project's tests
    on every pull request, so you know whether a change breaks anything
    *before* it's merged.
-   **Continuous deployment (CD)**: automatically building and publishing
    things, like your project's documentation or website, whenever changes are
    merged.

In fact, the website you're reading right now is built and deployed by a GitHub
Action every time I push a change to the course repository!

## Prerequisites

These tutorials build on things we've done earlier in the semester. You will need:

-   **conda**: If you don't have it, see the [Miniconda install
    instructions](../01_project_management/conda_install.qmd).
-   **git and a GitHub account**: You'll need to be able to clone, push, and
    pull from GitHub, and you should be comfortable with branches, forks, and
    pull requests. If you need a refresher, see the [git and GitHub
    tutorials](../02_git/index.qmd). In particular, you'll need to have set up
    authentication with GitHub, as described in
    [Part 2](../02_git/cli/exercise2.qmd#prerequisites-github-authentication).

The tutorials are written for the command line. If you prefer to use GitHub
Desktop for the `git` steps, that's fine; the GitHub Actions parts are the same
either way.
